howto.name: How to prepare for the Colorado ADMT and chatbot rules

steps.name: Decide whether you are covered
steps.text: Test each AI system that touches a consequential decision in Colorado against the proposed materially influences threshold, and each consumer chatbot against the companionship and business exemptions.

steps.name: Retire SB 24-205 language
steps.text: Replace duty of reasonable care provisions in policies and contracts with the ADMT Act's disclosure, adverse outcome notice, human review and correction duties.

steps.name: Comment by October 26
steps.text: File written comments through the Department of Law's comment form so they are received by 11:59 p.m. MST on October 26, 2026, or speak at the 10:00 a.m. hearing in Denver or on Zoom.

steps.name: Plan for January 1, 2027
steps.text: Build the notices, review process, age assurance and annual reporting the final rules will require.

short: The Colorado Attorney General's proposed rules for the ADMT Act and the Chatbot Safety Act: the timeline, what the rules do, how to comment before the October 26, 2026 hearing, and what changed from SB 24-205.
title: Colorado ADMT and Chatbot Safety Rulemaking
subtitle: The rules for SB 26-189 and HB 26-1263, hearing October 26, 2026
body_html:
On this page

  • Where it stands
  • The timeline
  • What the proposed rules do
  • How to comment
  • What changed from SB 24-205
  • Sources

Colorado is writing the rules for its two 2026 AI statutes now. The Attorney General filed one combined set of proposed rules, the Automated Decision-Making Technology and Conversational Artificial Intelligence Service Rules at 4 CCR 904-6, on August 11, 2026. They implement SB 26-189, the Automated Decision-Making Technology Act, which repealed and replaced the 2024 Colorado AI Act, and HB 26-1263, the Chatbot Safety Act. SB 26-189 and the rules, once final, take effect January 1, 2027. HB 26-1263 was signed on May 29, 2026 and took effect on August 12, 2026, and its duties for operators apply from January 1, 2027. This page tracks the rulemaking until it closes; the site's Colorado AI Act page covers the statutes.

Where it stands

The formal comment period is open. Written comments are considered if received by 11:59 p.m. MST on October 26, 2026, the day of the public rulemaking hearing; if the hearing is continued past October 26, the comment period runs to the last day of the hearing. The hearing starts at 10:00 a.m. on October 26 at 1300 Broadway, Room 1D, Denver, CO 80203, and can also be joined on Zoom, with registration through the Attorney General's AI rulemaking page. On October 6, 2026 the Department of Law released an interim draft of the rules with a cover page setting out additional considerations. The rules are proposed, not final: anything in them can still change at or after the hearing.

The timeline

DateStep
May 2026Governor Polis signs SB 26-189 (May 14) and HB 26-1263 (May 29)
June 23 to July 13, 2026Informal pre-rulemaking comment period
August 11, 2026The Department of Law files the Automated Decision-Making Technology and Conversational Artificial Intelligence Service rules, with the notice of hearing and statement of basis, with the Secretary of State; formal comment portal opens
August 12, 2026HB 26-1263 takes effect; its duties for operators apply from January 1, 2027
September 4, 2026Deadline for comments to be considered in a revised draft
October 6, 2026Interim draft of the rules released, with a cover page setting out additional considerations. The rules remain proposed, not final
October 26, 2026Public rulemaking hearing, 10:00 a.m., 1300 Broadway, Room 1D, Denver, CO 80203, or on Zoom with registration; written comments considered if received by 11:59 p.m. MST, or through the last hearing day if the hearing is continued
January 1, 2027SB 26-189 and the final rules take effect; HB 26-1263's operator duties apply

What the proposed rules do

For the ADMT Act. The rules set out when an automated decision-making technology "materially influences" a consequential decision, the threshold that decides whether a company is a covered developer or deployer; extend obligations to midstream developers; specify what a disclosure after an adverse outcome must contain; define what "meaningful human review" requires; and set the reporting duties and the process for consumers to request and correct inaccurate personal data used by the technology. Consequential decisions cover employment, lending, housing, insurance, health care, education and government services.

For the Chatbot Safety Act. The rules define which conversational AI services are "designed to simulate emotional companionship," which business-focused services are exempt, and what counts as commercially reasonable age assurance, disfavouring self-declared age or a government ID as the only method. They add detail on disclosures, protections for minors, crisis response, safeguards against prohibited content and the content of the operator's annual report. Rulemaking was mandatory under the ADMT Act. The Chatbot Safety Act does not require rules; the Attorney General included it in the package voluntarily, mainly to define what the operator's annual report must contain.

How to comment

Written comments go through the Colorado Department of Law's comment form for the ADMT Act and Chatbot Safety Act, linked from its AI rulemaking page, and are considered if received by 11:59 p.m. MST on October 26, 2026; if the hearing is continued past that day, written comments are taken through its last day. Comments at this stage enter the official rulemaking record. The hearing on October 26 starts at 10:00 a.m. and takes oral comment in person at 1300 Broadway, Room 1D, Denver, CO 80203, or on Zoom; Zoom participants register through the link on the Attorney General's page.

What changed from SB 24-205

SB 26-189 repealed and reenacted the 2024 Colorado AI Act before it ever took effect. The 2024 law's broad duty of reasonable care to avoid algorithmic discrimination is gone; the new act is narrower, centred on automated decision-making technology that materially influences a consequential decision, with disclosure, notice after an adverse outcome, human review and consumer correction rights. Guidance, contracts and compliance programmes written to SB 24-205's duty of care need revising against the new statute and these rules.

Sources

  • Colorado Department of Law, Colorado Anti-Discrimination in AI Law (ADAI) Rulemaking (coag.gov/ai/), and the ADMT Act and Chatbot Safety Act comment form. The August 11 filing, the October 6 interim draft, the comment deadline, and the hearing details on this page were checked against that page on October 18, 2026. That page gives July 1, 2026 as the date HB 26-1263 was signed, which conflicts with the legislature's record; this page follows the legislature.
  • Notice of rulemaking hearing and statement of basis, authority and purpose, filed August 11, 2026.
  • Colorado Legislative Council Staff, final fiscal note for HB 26-1263, July 13, 2026: signed into law May 29, 2026, takes effect August 12, 2026.
  • SB 26-189 and HB 26-1263, Colorado General Assembly, 2026 regular session.
  • Law firm alerts describing the proposed rules: Wiley (August 18, 2026), Husch Blackwell (August 19, 2026), Seyfarth Shaw (August 21, 2026), Ogletree Deakins.
